extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, literary critics, and philosophically inclined readers
extracted.subtask_description: Expository-philosophical literary prose outlining principles about symbols, silence, fantasy/imagination, human dignity, and social decline — useful as aesthetic and ethical guidance for writers and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence and Secrecy as conditions for thought and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "Silence and Secrecy!... Silence is the element in which great things fashion themselves together; that at length they may emerge, full-formed and majestic, into the daylight of Life... Bees will not work except in darkness; Thought will not work except in Silence: neither will Virtue work except in Secrecy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: hold your tongue for a time to gain clarity; avoid babbling of projects; secrecy preserves the root of virtue ("Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth"). Anti-pattern: publicizing nascent projects or prating to oneself, which stifles thought and withers the 'root' of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols combine concealment and revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: "In a Symbol there is concealment and yet revelation; here therefore, by Silence and by Speech acting together, comes a double significance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A symbol's power arises from the interplay of what it hides and what it shows. Examples: painted devices or simple seal-emblems where union of fit silence and high speech yields expressive force. Implication for creators: craft symbols that both veil and disclose, allowing layered meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy (imagination) as primary faculty over mere understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not our Logical, Mensurative faculty, but our Imaginative one is King over us; I might say, Priest and Prophet to lead us heavenward; or Magician and Wizard to lead us hellward."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination colors perception and gives purpose to sense; writers should privilege imaginative rendering rather than merely logical calculation. Examples: collective devotion to flags or crowns shows imaginative investment outweighing material value. Anti-pattern: reducing human motives to calculable 'motive-grinder' accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish extrinsic from intrinsic symbolic value
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of Symbols, however, I remark farther, that they have both an extrinsic and intrinsic value; oftenest the former only."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic symbols (e.g., clouted shoe, banners, coats-of-arms) unite people by accidental or conventional meaning; intrinsic symbols embody a 'Divine Idea' and are fit for deeper unity. For evaluators: ask whether a symbol has only accidental social power or an inherent, timeless resonance. Examples: military banners vs true works of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works of art as intrinsic symbols revealing the Infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: "In them (if thou know a Work of Art from a Daub of Artifice) wilt thou discern Eternity looking through Time; the Godlike rendered visible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for artistic worth: whether a work lets 'Eternity' look through Time — whether it reveals a larger, lasting truth. Examples: truly great epics and heroic lives; the Death of the Just as a perfected artistic symbol. Anti-pattern: artifice that only simulates depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of a symbol for collective veneration
rubrics_metrics.description: "When your Symbol has intrinsic meaning, and is of itself fit that men should unite round it... Then is it fit that men unite there; and worship together before such Symbol."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A symbol should be judged fit for collective worship or unity when it genuinely embodies the Godlike or eternal in a way perceivable to people; otherwise union around it will be accidental and unstable. Guidance: cultivate symbols that manifest universal or deep human truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist as creator/legislator of symbols; also as judge of obsolescence
rubrics_metrics.description: "A Hierarch, therefore, and Pontiff of the World will we call him, the Poet and inspired Maker... Such too will not always be wanting; neither perhaps now are. Meanwhile, as the average of matters goes, we account him Legislator and wise who can so much as tell when a Symbol has grown old, and gently remove it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role guidance: artists should both invent potent new symbols and discern when existing symbols are worn-out, removing them gently. Practical note: cultural stewardship requires both creation and careful pruning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols age; require reinterpretation to remain meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: "As Time adds much to the sacredness of Symbols, so likewise in his progress he at length defaces, or even desecrates them... Homer... needs a scientific telescope, it needs to be reinterpreted and artificially brought near us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for critics and translators: long-lived symbols may recede and require reinterpretation or scholarly effort to recover their force. Antipattern: assuming age alone guarantees continuing comprehensibility or relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant for eternity vs plant for day-and-year (targeting deep vs shallow faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wouldst thou plant for Eternity, then plant into the deep infinite faculties of man, his Fantasy and Heart; wouldst thou plant for Year and Day, then plant into his shallow superficial faculties, his Self-love and Arithmetical Understanding..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative guidance: aim your themes and symbols at deep human faculties (imagination, heart) for lasting work; targeting shallow appetites yields temporary, ephemeral influence. Editorial implication: prioritize depth over fashionable expedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor the toilworn craftsman and the spiritual artist
rubrics_metrics.description: "Two men I honor, and no third. First, the toilworn Craftsman... A second man I honor, and still more highly: Him who is seen toiling for the spiritually indispensable... Highest of all, when his outward and his inward endeavor are one: when we can name him Artist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical/aesthetic criterion: recognize dignity in both manual labor that secures daily bread and spiritual/artistic labor that secures cultural light; the ideal unites external toil and internal striving (peasant saint). For writers: depict dignity across social ranks; avoid contempt for crafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy as universal moral practice
rubrics_metrics.description: "In Good-breeding... it lies in human nature itself, and is due from all men towards all men... There is but one temple in the world... and that temple is the Body of Man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral guidance: politeness and reverence for human form are ethical obligations irrespective of rank. For social fiction or moral instruction, portray and practice courtesy widely. Warning: don't give respect indiscriminately when it's merely vanity-pocketed; exercise judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize hollow symbols and the Phoenix-like cycle of societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the chapters: many Church-Clothes and symbols have become 'mere hollow Shapes, or Masks' and 'rags and tatters of superannuated worn-out Symbols'; yet Society may undergo Phoenix death-and-rebirth, burning old garments to create new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical stance: be alert to when cultural forms are empty pageants; understand both the danger and inevitability of social transformation. Practical implication for writers: depict both the hollowing of symbols and the risks/necessities of their destruction and replacement; include awareness of collateral 'sparks' and human cost in renewal.
